newsitem.title: USA: Heavy decongestant use may cause strokes--study.
newsitem.headline: Heavy decongestant use may cause strokes--study.

text.p: Extensive use of common over-the-counter decongestants found in allergy medicines, cough syrup and health food supplements could cause strokes, according to a study.

A University of Pennsylvania Medical Center study presented at the American Academy of Neurology meeting in Boston showed decongestants like pseudoephedrine and phenylpropanolamine constricted the blood vessels in and around the nose to eliminate congestion.
"Decongestants can potentially affect blood vessels in both the brain and heart and can elevate blood pressure," senior study author Eric Raps, director of Penn's stroke program, said.

The pilot study examined eight stroke victims aged 36 to 60, who had not been considered at high risk for strokes. It found each had used over-the-counter decongestants for an extended period prior to the onset of symptoms.
Neuroradiologic imaging techniques including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), CT scans, angiography and doppler studies indicated constriction of blood vessels in the patients' brains, it showed.

Because laboratory tests for disease, malignancy and other infections were normal, researchers concluded the strokes could be related to the vasoconstrictive effects the over-the-counter decongestants had on the brain, it said.

"The study suggests it may be possible to identify patients who run a higher risk of stroke when using decongestants," lead study author Lidgia Vives, a stroke and neurointensive care fellow at the University of Pennsylvania Medical Center, said.
Individuals whose blood vessels had a tendency to constrict easier than others could be more sensitive to decongestants, the pilot study said.

Conditions which suggested this tendency included migraines, livedo reticularis, or a bluish, net-like discoloration of the skin, and Raynaud's Phenomenon, which is a change in the color of the skin triggered by exposure to cold weather, the study said.
